Grandparent is Sick

When a grandparent is seriously ill, this story walks alongside your child through changed visits and unfamiliar feelings, without ever forcing the hardest questions.

A personalized picture book in which your child is the hero — and masters this challenge themselves. The first story is free.

Create This Story

The visit to Grandma suddenly looks different: she now sits in a wheelchair, sleeps through the afternoon, doesn't always recognize names right away, or there's a hospital bed newly set up in the living room. Your child senses that something has changed but often can't place it — and may ask, out of nowhere, right at the family table: “Will Grandpa get better again?” In that moment you find yourself caught between your own worry and grief and the task of answering your child honestly, but gently.

Children this age notice precisely when adults are keeping something from them. When questions go unanswered, children often fill the gap with their own, usually worse, imaginings, or quietly hold themselves responsible for the changed mood at home. At the same time, a serious illness in the closest circle is hard for a child to grasp, because familiar roles shift: the once-strong grandfather suddenly needs help himself, and even their own parents seem more exhausted and distant than usual.

A story brings the unspoken gently into the light. Through a character living through a similar change in their closest circle, feelings like fear, confusion or even anger become speakable, without your child having to name them first. They see someone else managing the very same conflicting feelings — being sad and still allowed to keep playing, for instance. And because the book can be picked up again and again, your child can return to it whenever a new question or a new visit comes up.

In the personalized story, your child — with their own face on every page — accompanies a beloved grandmother or grandfather figure through changed visits: the hospital bed, the wheelchair, the shorter, quieter moments together. The story does not push dying as a topic, but it also does not hide that some things are serious and have changed. It shows what stays: looking through old photos together, holding a hand, hearing a familiar voice. The first story is free, so you can check whether it fits your family's situation.

For home: answer your child's questions as honestly as they are asked, without getting ahead of them toward a possible death — follow your child's own pace. Prepare a visit briefly beforehand by describing concretely what your child will see (tubes, a wheelchair, a quieter conversation), so nothing comes as a shock. Let your child take part in their own way — a drawing, a short visit, a video call if a longer visit would be too much. If your child withdraws strongly, starts wetting the bed again, becomes aggressive, or barely mentions the grandparent for weeks, seek advice from your paediatrician or a family counselling service.

What your child learns

Naming feelings, coping with change, showing closeness, feeling free to ask questions, family togetherness.

Recommended age

4-10 years

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I tell my child that grandpa might die?

Follow your child's own questions rather than raising the possibility unprompted — forcing the subject before a child is ready can overwhelm more than it helps. If your child does ask directly, answer honestly in simple words rather than deflecting, since evasive answers usually raise more anxiety than a gentle truth.

How do I prepare my child for a hospital or care-home visit?

Describe beforehand, in concrete terms, what your child will see and hear — tubes, machines, a quieter or slower grandparent — so the room itself doesn't come as the first shock. Keep the visit short and let your child decide how close they want to get; a drawing handed over from a distance is still a real visit.

My child seems unaffected and keeps playing as normal — is that a problem?

No, this is a common and healthy way for children to process difficult family situations in small doses rather than all at once. Play is not indifference; it's often exactly how a child takes a break from something too big to hold onto for long. Stay available for the moments when questions do surface.

What if my child asks the same question over and over?

Answer patiently and consistently each time, even if it feels repetitive to you — repetition is how children build understanding of something this big, not a sign they didn't listen. Keep your answers simple and stable rather than adding new details each round, so the picture stays clear.

When should we get outside help for our child?

If your child withdraws strongly for weeks, regresses noticeably (bedwetting, clinginess), becomes unusually aggressive, or refuses entirely to talk about the grandparent, it's worth talking to your paediatrician or a family counselling service. They can assess whether your child needs extra support in processing the situation.
